Chapter 9 Vibration of a system with one degree of freedom (nihanje sistema z eno prostostno stopnjo)

Chapter 9Lecture: Vibration of a system with one degree of freedom (nihanje sistema z eno prostostno stopnjo)

1 A hammer blow: why it swings and why it comes to rest

Let us take a wall and clamp a steel cantilever in it, 1 m long. To the free end we fix a weight of mass 50 kg. This is our system A. We hit the tip with a hammer. The size of the blow, 5 N s, is explained in the third part, here it only says that the weight gets the velocity 0.1 m/s. Then we record how high the tip is at every moment. What will we see?

We draw a horizontal axis for time in seconds and a vertical axis for the height of the tip \(q\) in millimetres. Right after the blow the tip swings up and down, about eleven times in two seconds. But the peaks are not equally high. Let us join them with a dashed curve, the envelope: the first peak is at 2.82 mm, then each one is a little lower. When is a peak only half as high? At 1.41 mm, after 1.957 s.

There are three questions in this picture. Why does the tip swing instead of just going back? Why always with the same rhythm? And why do the peaks fall so evenly?

The answer in one sentence: left alone, the system does two things at once, it swings with its own frequency \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \sqrt{k/m}\), set by the beam and the weight, and each swing is smaller than the last by the same share, set by the damping. Two numbers, \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) and the damping ratio \(\zeta\) (razmernik dušenja), say everything. Now we go down to the reasons.

1.1 Why is one equation with three terms enough?

The cantilever has infinitely many points. How many numbers must we know to say where all of it is? We claim that one is enough, and that one equation holds for it. We start at the wall the cantilever is clamped in. From it we draw a straight dashed line, the cantilever at rest. Now let the cantilever be bent upwards. At its end there is the weight of mass \(m\). How far is the tip raised? By \(q\), measured from rest.

Does one number \(q\) really tell where the whole beam is? We assume that the beam always bends into the same shape, the one a force at the end gives, and only its size changes. Why may we? The weight of 50 kg is much heavier than the part of the beam that moves with it, which counts only 1.47 kg. When may we not? With a light weight, or with a blow so sharp that it excites the second shape of the beam, which vibrates at 143 Hz, 26 times faster than the first. What does the choice cost? If we count the mass of the beam, this changes:

\[m:\ 50\ \text{kg} \to 51.47\ \text{kg} , \qquad f_{\mathrm{n}}:\ 5.637\ \text{Hz} \to 5.556\ \text{Hz}\ \ (-1.4\ \%) .\]

In the book: 9.1.1, (9.4).

Which forces act on the weight? We cut the weight out and draw it alone. Say it is just moving up with velocity \(\dot q\). The bent beam pulls it back towards rest with the force \(k q\). Why in proportion to \(q\)? A ruler that we bend over the edge of a table twice as far pushes us back twice as hard. For the cantilever this is the stiffness \(k\) from the chapter on beams, \(k = 3EI/L^3 = 62\,720\) N/m, (9.3).

Where is the weight's gravity? We measure \(q\) from the position in which the weight hangs at rest. There the beam already carries the weight. Since the beam's force is proportional to the bending, the extra bending \(q\) adds exactly \(k q\), and gravity drops out of the equation with no error.

The second force is the damping force \(c\dot q\), pointing against the velocity. In the model it is drawn by a damper of coefficient \(c\) between the weight and the ground. Now Newton comes in: mass times acceleration is the sum of the forces. We write it on the board: \(m\ddot q = -k q - c\dot q\). We move the terms to the left and get the equation with three terms,

\[m\,\ddot q + c\,\dot q + k\,q = 0 .\]

In the book: 9.1.3, (9.8).

One last assumption of this step: the displacements are small. Why may we? The tip moves by millimetres, the beam is a metre long. When not? At large displacements, for example a pendulum at a large angle. What does it cost? The dropped terms are the remainder \(R\) in (9.7), bounded by terms of second order, squares and products of the displacement, the velocity and the acceleration. A swing half as large therefore means an error four times smaller.

1.2 Why does the damping force grow with the speed?

What is a damper? We draw a piston in a cylinder of oil that joins the point \(A\) and the point \(B\) at the distance \(\ell\). Let us pull \(B\) away from \(A\), in the direction \(\vek e\). The oil resists, so a force towards \(A\) acts on \(B\), and an equal force towards \(B\) on \(A\).

How large is this force? Think of a hand pulled through water: the faster we pull it, the harder it resists. We draw an axis of velocity and an axis of force. The viscous damper is the one whose force is a straight line through the origin with slope \(-c\). Twice as fast, twice as hard. In the book: 9.1.2.

1.3 Why does it swing at all instead of just returning?

We lift the weight and let it go. The beam pulls it back towards rest. Why does it not stop there, but go on to the other side? Let us set the damping aside for a moment and follow the weight through one swing. We draw four times the wall and the cantilever at rest. In position 1 the tip is up and stands still for an instant. The beam is bent, so it pulls it down with the force \(k q\). The weight speeds up downwards.

In position 2 the cantilever is straight again. The beam's force is zero here. Does the weight stop here? No, it has been speeding up downwards all the time, so now it is at its fastest, with velocity \(\dot q\) downwards. A moving body keeps moving until a force stops it. This is Newton's first law, and we feel it on a swing that passes the lowest point and does not stay there.

So the weight overshoots equilibrium and goes on to the other side. In position 3 the tip is down and again stands still for an instant. Now the beam pulls it up. In position 4 the cantilever is straight once more, and the weight is at its fastest upwards. And we are back at position 1.

What happens to the energy? In positions 1 and 3 it is all in the bent beam, in positions 2 and 4 it is all in the motion of the weight. Twice in every swing it changes form. Let us draw this another way. Let one axis be the displacement \(q\) and the other the velocity \(\dot q/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\). Each position is now a point: 1 on the right, 2 at the bottom, 3 on the left, 4 at the top. Without damping the energy is conserved and the point runs round a circle, again and again. In the book: 9.48, 9.51, point 2.

1.4 Why exactly the frequency \(\sqrt{k/m}\)?

Where does the rhythm come from, eleven swings in two seconds and not five or fifty? Back to the record of the blow. A stiffer beam pulls the weight back harder, so it returns sooner. A heavier weight is harder to turn round, so it is slower. The rhythm therefore depends on \(k\) and \(m\). We divide the equation without damping by \(m\), \(\ddot q + (k/m)\,q = 0\), and only the ratio \(k/m\) is left in it, whose unit is 1/s². A number that says how fast something happens has the unit 1/s, so we take the root. For system A we write it on the board:

\[\frac{k}{m} = \frac{62\,720}{50} = 1254.4\ \frac{1}{\text{s}^2} , \qquad \omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \sqrt{1254.4} = 35.4175\ \frac{1}{\text{s}} ,\]
\[T_{\mathrm{n}} = \frac{2\pi}{\omega_{\mathrm{n}}} = 0.1774\ \text{s} , \qquad f_{\mathrm{n}} = \frac{1}{T_{\mathrm{n}}} = 5.637\ \text{Hz} .\]

We count the swings in the record: there are 11 in 1.957 s, which is indeed 0.1774 s per swing.

Why is it called natural (lastna)? Because the system chooses it by itself. A harder blow gives higher peaks, but the rhythm stays the same. In the book: 9.1.4, 9.4, (9.9).

1.5 Why does each swing shrink by the same share?

The peaks in the record get lower. Does each swing lose the same height or the same share of its height? Let us see what the damper does. We draw again the axis of displacement and the axis of velocity and the start at the point \((q_0, 0)\), a displacement without velocity. Without damping the point runs round the circle. Now we add the damper. Its force is proportional to the velocity, so it takes energy at the rate \(c\dot q^2\).

Let us compare a large swing, one run round the circle, with one half as large, a run round a circle of half the radius. In the smaller one the weight is half as fast everywhere, so it loses a quarter of the energy the large swing loses. But it also has only a quarter of its energy, since the energy at the end of a swing is \(\tfrac12 k q^2\), so at half the \(q\) a quarter. The share lost is therefore the same. So the point comes closer to the centre by the same share in every turn, and the circle becomes a spiral. The picture draws it for \(\zeta = 0.1\), since for system A we would need 11 turns to get to half.

Where is this in the record of the blow? The same share in equal times is exactly what the exponential function does. That is why the peaks lie on the exponential envelope. For system A the ratio of two successive peaks is

\[\mathrm{e}^{-2\pi\zeta/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}} = \mathrm{e}^{-2\pi\cdot 0.01/\sqrt{0.9999}} = 0.939 ,\]

each peak is 6.1 % lower than the one before. After 11 swings \(0.939^{11} = 0.50\), so the envelope is at half after 1.957 s. In the book: 9.51, (9.51).

What is the key here? That everything in the equation is proportional to \(q\) and its derivatives. A smaller motion is the same motion, only scaled down. And that is an assumption about the damper.

Why is the viscous damper the right model? With it the equation stays linear and can be solved to the end, and it describes a piston in oil well. When is it not? With dry friction in joints, where the force has a constant size. On axes of time and displacement we draw such a motion: the peaks now lie not on an exponential curve but on two straight lines. A swing loses not the same share but the same height, and the motion stops in a band around equilibrium, \(u_{\mathrm{D}}\) wide on each side, where the beam no longer overcomes the friction. Below, the end of the motion is drawn enlarged. What does the assumption cost? If there is dry friction in the system, the rule "the same share per swing" fails. In the book: 9.14.4.

1.6 Why is there a critical damping?

How strong is the damper of system A? Let us compare the largest damper force with the largest beam force in one swing. Their ratio is \(c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}/k = 2\zeta\), at \(\zeta = 0.01\) that is 2 %. And what if we make the damper stronger?

We draw an axis of time and an axis of displacement. We displace the weight by 1 mm and let it go. At \(\zeta = 0.1\) it still swings: it passes equilibrium at 0.0474 s and reaches \(-0.729\) mm on the other side at 0.0891 s, then decays under the envelope. At \(\zeta = 1\) the damper brakes the weight on its way back so hard that it arrives at equilibrium with no speed and does not cross it. This is critical damping (kritično dušenje),

\[c_{\mathrm{kr}} = 2\sqrt{k m} = 2\sqrt{62\,720 \cdot 50} = 3541.75\ \text{N s/m} .\]

At \(\zeta = 2\) the weight returns even more slowly. More damping than critical only slows the return.

We have all seen this in a door closer. With too little oil the door slams and bounces back, with too much it creeps. Critical damping is the border between the two. In the book: 9.5, (9.10), 9.50, 9.51, points 3 and 4.

1.7 Back up: from three forces to the record of the blow

Now we have the ground: Newton's laws, a beam that resists in proportion to its bending, and a damper that resists in proportion to the speed. Let us put the story back together. The beam and the weight alone give an endless run round the circle at the rhythm \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 35.4175\) 1/s. We add a weak damper, only 2 % of the beam's force.

Does the damper change the rhythm? Hardly. The damped frequency is \(\omega_{\mathrm{d}} = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}\), and since \(\zeta\) enters squared,

\[\omega_{\mathrm{d}} = 35.4157\ \frac{1}{\text{s}} \quad \text{against} \quad \omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 35.4175\ \frac{1}{\text{s}} ,\]

a difference of 0.005 %. This is the assumption \(\omega_{\mathrm{d}} \approx \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\). When does it fail? At \(\zeta = 0.5\) we get \(\sqrt{0.75} = 0.866\), the frequency drops by 13 %.

But the damper takes the same share of energy in every turn, so the circle becomes a spiral. And in the record of the blow this is exactly our first picture: a cosine at the natural frequency inside a falling exponential envelope. In the book: (9.48), 9.49.

1.8 By hand and eye

Whoever has only two minutes should remember the four positions. At the ends the force is largest and the velocity zero, in the middle the velocity is largest and the force zero. So the weight always overshoots equilibrium. This view adds the answer to why it swings at all.

1.9 By energy

In the phase plane the energy is proportional to the squared distance from the centre. The circle is constant energy, the spiral is energy that falls by the same share in every turn. This view adds why the decay is the same share per swing and why the frequency does not depend on the strength of the blow: a bigger blow is only a bigger circle, and going round takes the same time.

1.10 By algebra

The idea is one: we try \(q = \mathrm{e}^{st}\). The equation then shrinks to \(m s^2 + c s + k = 0\), and we look for its roots \(s = -\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}} \pm \mathrm{i}\,\omega_{\mathrm{d}}\). We draw the real axis and the imaginary axis. At small damping the roots are on an arc to the left of the imaginary axis. The distance to the left of the axis is the rate of decay, \(\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 0.354\) 1/s for system A, the height is the frequency \(\omega_{\mathrm{d}}\). As \(\zeta\) grows, the roots meet on the real axis: this is critical damping. Above it they move apart along the real axis and there is no vibration any more. This view adds that one picture shows both numbers at once. In the book: 9.5, 9.48.

1.11 By numbers

For system A from the same start we write on the board:

\(\zeta\) \(c\) (N s/m) roots \(s\) (1/s) motion
0.1 354.2 \(-3.5418 \pm 35.2400\,\mathrm{i}\) swings
1 3541.8 \(-35.4175\) (double) does not cross equilibrium
2 7083.5 \(-9.4901\) and \(-132.1799\) returns slowly

The imaginary part of a root is the frequency we see in the curve, the real part the rate at which the curve decays. This view adds how large the numbers are for a real system. In the book: 9.50.

2 Resonance: why 20 N swings the cantilever fifty times further

Take again our steel cantilever with a weight at its tip, system A from the previous part, with a weight of mass 50 kg. Press on the tip with a force of 20 N and hold it there. How far does the tip move? By \(Q_0/k = 0.319\) mm, the static displacement (statični pomik), barely a third of a millimetre. Now let the same 20 N go back and forth like a cosine, \(Q(t) = Q_0\cos\Omega t\), as a machine turning next to the cantilever gives it. If the machine turns slowly, at half the natural frequency, so \(r = \Omega/\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 0.5\), the swing is \(0.425\) mm, a little more than static. If it turns fast, at \(r = 2\), the swing is only \(0.106\) mm. But at \(r = 1\), when the force swings 5.6 times a second, the tip swings by \(15.944\) mm. The force is no larger. Where does the factor 50 come from, and why only at this one frequency?

The answer in one sentence: in steady swinging the force must make up at every instant what the spring, the damper and the mass ask for, and at the natural frequency the spring gives exactly what the mass needs, so the force is left with only the small damper and the swing grows until the damper alone balances it. Let us draw this claim.

First we draw the horizontal axis at \(r = 1\). On it is the force \(Q_0\), a blackwhite arrow. Newton's law says the force must at every instant be the sum of three terms, the spring, the damper and the inertia term. We lay them head to tail. First the spring term \(kZ\), which points along the displacement. Then the damper term \(\mathrm{i}\,c\,\Omega Z\), turned a quarter turn. We draw it at \(\zeta = 0.25\), since at system A's damping, \(\zeta = 0.01\), it would be fifty times shorter than the force and we would not see it. And last the inertia term \(-m\Omega^2 Z\), which points back, against the spring term. Do you see what happened? The spring and inertia terms are equally long and cancel. The force \(Q_0\) must be covered by the damper arrow alone. The displacement is therefore a quarter turn behind the force, \(\varphi = 90^\circ\). This picture is the answer. Now let us ask why each of its parts is as it is.

In the book: 9.6.

2.1 Why does the system swing at the force's frequency and not its own?

We drew the polygon as if the cantilever swings at the same frequency as the force. But the cantilever has its own natural frequency. Why does it not use it? Let us look at what happens when we switch the machine on. We draw the graph of the displacement in time, first without damping. At \(r = 0.9\) the displacement beats: the swing grows and shrinks under an envelope that repeats every \(1.774\) s. It is the sum of two swings, the forced one at the force's frequency and the free one at its own, which now add and now subtract.

Now we add damping, the lower graph with \(\zeta = 0.01\). The displacement is again the sum of both. But the free part is just what we watched in the previous part: the swing after a blow, which with damping dies out with the envelope \(\mathrm{e}^{-\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t}\). For system A this envelope is below one percent after \(13.00\) s. What is left? Only the forced part, the steady state (ustaljeno stanje), which swings at the force's frequency whatever the start.

With this we have assumed something: from now on we look only at the steady state. Why may we? Because the free part dies out. When may we not? Right after switching on, and near resonance with little damping, where the swing grows over many swings. What does it cost? At first the cantilever can beat and the swing differs from the steady one: without damping the envelope of the beating reaches \(3.357\) mm, while the steady swing is only \(1.6708\) mm, half as much.

In the book: 9.62, points 2 and 3.

2.2 Why do the three terms point a quarter turn apart?

The polygon needs the spring, damper and inertia terms to point in directions a quarter turn apart. Where does this come from? Think of a swing. Where is it fastest? In the middle. Where does it stand still? At the ends. That is our ground, and we read everything from it.

We draw the axis and the circle on which an arrow turns. The displacement arrow, of length \(X\), turns with angular speed \(\Omega\). What we see on the cantilever is its shadow on the horizontal axis, the displacement \(q\). As the arrow turns, the shadow walks back and forth. Next to it we draw a time axis and on it the displacement \(q\) in time, a cosine. At the start of the period the displacement is at the end of the swing. There the tip stands still, so the velocity \(\dot q\) is exactly zero. When passing the middle the velocity is largest. So the velocity peaks a quarter period before the displacement. On the circle this is the velocity arrow \(\Omega X\), a quarter turn ahead of the displacement arrow.

And the acceleration? At the end of the swing the tip is pulled back towards the middle, so the acceleration \(\ddot q\) is largest there and points against the displacement. On the circle it is the acceleration arrow \(\Omega^2 X\), turned half a turn. Now back to the polygon. The spring force \(kq\) follows the displacement, the damper force \(c\dot q\) follows the velocity, the inertia term \(m\ddot q\) follows the acceleration. Three directions, each a quarter turn further. Every derivative turns the arrow a quarter turn and multiplies it by \(\Omega\).

In the book: 9.3.2, 9.32.

2.3 Why do spring and mass cancel at \(\Omega = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\)?

The factor 50 appears at one frequency only. What is so special about \(r = 1\)? Back to the polygon at \(r = 1\). The spring term is \(kX\) long, the inertia term \(m\Omega^2 X\), and points the other way. When are they equally long? When \(k = m\Omega^2\), so \(\Omega^2 = k/m\). And that is exactly the natural circular frequency, \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 = k/m\). Not a coincidence, it is what natural frequency means: in the free swing of the previous part the spring by itself gives exactly the force the mass needs to turn round, with no outside help. Pushed at that rhythm, the cantilever swings by itself, and the force is left with only the damper.

So how large is \(X\)? The damper arrow must be as long as the force \(Q_0\), so \(c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X = Q_0\). We write on the board:

\[c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 1254.40\ \text{N/m}, \qquad X = \frac{Q_0}{c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}} = \frac{20}{1254.40}\ \text{m} = 15.944\ \text{mm}, \qquad \frac{X}{Q_0/k} = \frac{k}{c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}} = \frac{1}{2\zeta} = 50 .\]

That is the swing in our picture at the top, fifty times the static displacement.

In the book: 9.64, (9.66).

2.4 Why does the swing grow, and what stops it?

At \(r = 1\) the force is left with only the damper. But why does the swing then grow to fifty times the static one instead of staying small? And what stops it in the end? At \(r = 1\) the displacement is a quarter turn behind the force. The velocity is a quarter turn ahead of the displacement. What follows? The force is exactly in step with the velocity: it pushes forward when the weight moves forward and back when it moves back. Like a child on a swing whom we push always at the right moment. The ground of this answer is the meaning of work: a force that pushes along the motion adds energy.

What happens without damping? We draw the graph of the displacement in time. The displacement from rest grows without end, between the lines \(\pm Q_0 t/(2m\omega_{\mathrm{n}})\), which move apart by \(\pi Q_0/k = 1.0018\) mm in every swing. With damping the growth stops at \(15.944\) mm. The lower line at \(10.887\) mm, which the displacement reaches after \(1.928\) s, we keep in mind for the end. Why exactly there?

We draw time in periods of the force and upwards power in watts. How much power does the force put in? Power is force times velocity. The force is a constant 20 N and the velocity is proportional to the swing, so the power put in grows in proportion to the swing. How much does the damper take? Its power is \(c\dot q^2\) and grows with the square of the swing. At a small swing the force puts in more than the damper takes, and the swing grows. But a square catches up with a straight line. At a swing of \(15.944\) mm the power put in and the power lost are equal at every instant, one single curve, with the average \(5.647\) W. The stored energy \(7.972\) J therefore no longer changes. For comparison, on the right the same at \(r = 0.9\): the power put in is negative part of the time, the force then takes energy away, the power lost never is. The averages are again equal, but only \(0.0502\) W, 112 times less for the same force, and the energy only wobbles slightly.

Here we assumed that there is damping. What if there is none? Then there is no steady state at \(r = 1\) and the swing grows without bound. What does the size of the damping do? The peak is \(1/(2\zeta)\), so half the damping means twice the swing. Far from resonance damping hardly matters: the damper arrow at \(r = 0.5\) and at \(r = 2\) is short.

In the book: 9.67, 9.7.1.

2.5 Why does the response follow the force below resonance and oppose it above?

And away from resonance? Why does the tip follow a slow force and move against a fast one? We draw the polygon at \(r = 0.5\), with the same force \(Q_0\). The spring term is long, the inertia term only a quarter of it, since the ratio \(m\Omega^2/k = r^2 = 0.25\). In slow motion the mass needs little force, so the spring carries almost all of it, almost as in statics. The damper term is short and the lag \(\varphi\) small, for system A only \(0.76^\circ\) (larger in the picture, which is drawn at \(\zeta = 0.25\)). The swing is \(1.33\) times static.

Now the polygon at \(r = 2\), again with the same force. The inertia term is four times longer than the spring term. The force goes almost all into shaking the mass. And a mass shaken fast is always on the other side from where the force pulls, since the acceleration points against the displacement. The lag is almost half a turn, \(179.24^\circ\), the swing only a third of static.

Let us see the same in time. At \(r = 0.5\) the force and the response nearly coincide. At \(r = 1\) the peak of the response comes after the peak of the force, by a quarter swing. At \(r = 2\) the response is just opposite to the force, the lag is almost half a swing. Try it at home: hang a weight on a rubber band. Move your hand slowly and the weight follows. Shake it fast and the weight nearly stands still while your hand moves against it.

In the book: 9.69.

2.6 Back up: from the polygon the whole curve

Now we have all the pieces. The polygon is a right triangle: one leg is the difference of the spring and inertia terms, \((k - m\Omega^2)X\), the other is the damper term \(c\,\Omega X\), and the hypotenuse is the force \(Q_0\). Pythagoras gives

\[Q_0^2 = (k - m\Omega^2)^2 X^2 + (c\,\Omega)^2 X^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad D = \frac{X}{Q_0/k} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(1 - r^2)^2 + (2\zeta r)^2}} .\]

We draw it on the axes \(r\) and \(D\). For a slow force \(D = 1\), the static displacement. The blue curve of system A rises at \(r = 1\) to 50 and then falls below 1. Our three polygons are just three points on this curve. The other curves are for larger damping: more damping, a lower peak. An engineer reads a rule from it: the machine's speed should be far from \(r = 1\).

Is the peak really exactly at \(r = 1\)? Nearly. The peaks are in fact at \(r = \sqrt{1 - 2\zeta^2}\). Why may we still say \(r = 1\)? For system A the peak is at \(r = 0.99990\) and \(D_{\max} = 50.0025\), only \(0.005\ \%\) above 50. When may we not? At larger damping: at \(\zeta = 0.2\) the peak is at \(r = 0.95917\), and from \(\zeta \ge 1/\sqrt2\) there is no peak at all.

In the book: 9.64, 9.8.2.

2.7 Four perspectives

The geometric perspective is the polygon at \(r = 1\). This is the few minute explanation: one right triangle gives the swing and the lag.

The perspective by hand and energy is the balance of power. It adds what the polygon does not say: the swing needs time to grow, and the damping sets its height.

The algebraic perspective: try \(q = Z\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\). Every derivative becomes a multiplication by \(\mathrm{i}\Omega\), as we saw with the turning arrows, and the equation becomes an ordinary equation for \(Z\), with the solution \(Z = Q_0 H(\Omega)\), \(H = 1/(k - m\Omega^2 + \mathrm{i}\,c\,\Omega)\). The polygon is this complex number, drawn. In the book: 9.61, 9.62.

The perspective by numbers is our first picture, now read as a table:

\(r\) \(D\) \(X\) (mm) \(\varphi\)
\(0.5\) \(1.33\) \(0.425\) \(0.76^\circ\)
\(1\) \(50\) \(15.944\) \(90^\circ\)
\(2\) \(0.33\) \(0.106\) \(179.24^\circ\)

The swing at \(r = 0.5\), at \(r = 1\) and at \(r = 2\) are drawn at the same scale, so the eye sees the ratio 50 to 1.

2.8 Assumptions: why they hold, when not, and what they cost

Three assumptions were stated where they entered: the steady state, the damping and the peak at \(r = 1\). Three are left that hold for the whole of today's part.

A linear model with one shape. We draw the amplitude against frequency. The blue curve is our model. If we also take part of the beam's mass, the peak moves from \(5.637\) Hz to \(5.556\) Hz. A sharp peak makes a small model error large: at \(5.637\) Hz the cantilever with the beam's mass is already well below its own peak.

And the most important one, at the end. The model promises \(15.944\) mm. At that swing the alternating stress at the clamp is \(15.944 \cdot 11.760 = 187.5\) MPa, on top of \(91.97\) MPa from the weight, \(279.5\) MPa in all. That is above the yield stress of \(220\) MPa. The linear model itself says it has left its range. It holds only up to a swing of \(10.887\) mm, that is \(D \le 34.14\), so outside the band from \(5.5757\) to \(5.6963\) Hz, \(2.14\ \%\) of the natural frequency wide. On the growth graph this limit is reached without damping after \(1.928\) s. Outside this narrow band the model holds, inside it only for a smaller force.

The force amplitude is 20 N at every frequency. With a machine with an unbalanced rotor, however, the force grows with \(\Omega^2\) and the curve in the picture of \(D(r)\) changes. In the book: 9.8.1.

3 Any force: a sum of hammer blows

So far we have struck cantilever A once and let it swing. Then we pushed it in a steady rhythm with a cosine. A real force is neither. A force gauge under the weight records a jagged curve that never repeats. Do we need a new theory for every shape of force? The answer is no, and today we see why. The whole answer is on one picture.

First we draw three horizontal axes, all with the same time. On the top one we draw the force \(Q(s)\), a single wave that rises to 20 N and lasts the time \(t_{\mathrm{p}}\), half the natural period. Now we cut it into strips (trakovi), six of them here. Each is \(\Delta s\) wide, here \(0.0148\) s, and has its own instant \(s_{\mathrm{j}}\) in the middle. What does a single strip do? It strikes the weight, like a hammer, and the weight swings. Each strip sets off its own small swing, which starts at its \(s_{\mathrm{j}}\). We simply add these six swings and get the motion of the cantilever.

That is today's claim. Every short piece of force is a small hammer blow. We already know the answer to a blow: the free swing of the first part, scaled by the size of the blow and shifted to its instant. We just add the answers:

\[q(t) \approx \sum_{\mathrm{s}_\mathrm{j} \le \mathrm{t}} h(t - s_{\mathrm{j}})\,Q(s_{\mathrm{j}})\,\Delta s .\]

As the strips get thinner, the sum becomes an integral, \(q(t) = \int_0^t h(t - s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\). In the book: 9.10.1.

The claim has four steps that are not self-evident. Why does only the area of a strip count? Why is the answer exactly the free swing? Why may we add the answers? And why does \(t - s\) stand in the integral? Let us go one at a time.

3.1 Why does only the impulse of a short push count, not its shape?

A strip of force has a height and a width. Must we know both, or is one number enough? We take a force axis and a time axis, and below them the response axes, where we draw the motion of the weight. We draw a push that lasts a quarter of the natural period, \(T_{\mathrm{n}}/4\), low and long, and below it its response. Then a push of length \(T_{\mathrm{n}}/10\), two and a half times taller, with its response. Then a push of length \(T_{\mathrm{n}}/50\), tall and narrow, and its response. All three have the same area, force times time is the same for all. We call this area the impulse (impulz) \(I\).

What happens to the weight during a short push? The weight gains speed, but it has hardly any time to move. Let us write on the board the book's numbers for a force of \(490.5\) N, the weight of the \(50\) kg mass:

length of the push displacement during the push spring force at its end
\(T_{\mathrm{n}}/10\) at most \(1.5\) mm
\(T_{\mathrm{n}}/50\) at most \(0.062\) mm at most \(3.9\) N

A spring force of \(3.9\) N against a push of \(490.5\) N is almost nothing. During the push the spring and the damper have nothing to answer to yet. What remains is Newton's second law: force times a short time is mass times the change of speed, \(m\,\Delta\dot q = I\). We have all felt this when kicking a ball. The kick is short, the ball flies off with some speed, but during the kick it hardly moves.

So it does not matter whether the push is tall and short or low and long. The area counts. Let us look below, on the response axes. The response to the longest push is still visibly different, while the response to the shortest almost covers the dashed curve, the answer to a pure blow. In the book: 9.9.3 and lemma 9.87.

Here an assumption came in: the push, and later every strip of force, is short compared to \(T_{\mathrm{n}}\). We used it with the pushes of equal area. Why it holds: during a short strip the weight does not move, and our strips, \(0.0148\) s wide, are shorter than \(T_{\mathrm{n}}/10 = 0.0177\) s. What it does to the result: a rectangle of length \(\varepsilon\) answers like the blow multiplied by \(\sin\theta/\theta\), \(\theta = \pi\varepsilon/T_{\mathrm{n}}\), and delayed by \(\varepsilon/2\). At \(\varepsilon = T_{\mathrm{n}}/10\) the factor is \(0.984\), the response is \(1.6\) % smaller. At \(\varepsilon = T_{\mathrm{n}}/4\) it is \(10\) % smaller and delayed by \(T_{\mathrm{n}}/8\). When not: a push lasting a good part of \(T_{\mathrm{n}}\). Then the shape counts. In the book: equations (9.87) and (9.88).

3.2 Why is the answer to a blow the free swing?

What is left after the blow? No outside force acts any more. The weight is at its equilibrium position and has the speed \(I/m\). That is exactly the problem of the first part: a free swing that starts at position zero with speed \(I/m\). For a blow of \(1\) N s we give it a name, the impulse response (impulzni odziv) \(h\). We draw a time axis and on it the swing \(h(u)\), which starts at zero, since at the blow the weight has not moved yet. Its peaks are bounded by the envelope, which decays because of damping. In the first part a blow of \(5\) N s on \(50\) kg gave a speed of \(0.1\) m/s, and that was the same curve, five times larger. In the book: definition 9.86, equation (9.84).

3.3 Why may we add the answers?

We strike twice, the second time while the cantilever is still swinging from the first blow. Does the second blow disturb the swing the first one set off? This is the most important step, so we draw it on its own, with two blows.

We draw three time axes, one below the other. On the top one we strike the weight at time zero with a blow \(I_1 = 5\) N s. The weight swings, the free swing of the previous step. On the middle axis we have the same cantilever, but we strike it later, at \(0.16\) s, with \(I_2 = 3\) N s. This blow too sets off its own swing, which is zero before the blow.

Now, at the bottom, we strike with both blows, each at its time. What does the cantilever do? We pick the instant \(t = 0.21\) s. At the top the displacement then is \(q_1 = 2.4\) mm, in the middle \(q_2 = 1.6\) mm. At the bottom we stack them one on the other and get \(q_1 + q_2 = 4.0\) mm. We do this at every instant and get the blue curve. We claim that this really is the motion of the cantilever under both blows. Why?

Let us look at what the equation adds. The spring force is \(k\,q\): twice the bend, twice the force. That is a measured fact for small bends. The damper force is \(c\,\dot q\): twice the speed, twice the force. The inertia is \(m\,\ddot q\). Every term is proportional to the motion. If motion \(q_1\) balances the force of the first blow and motion \(q_2\) that of the second, then the spring force at the displacement \(q_1 + q_2\) is nothing but the spring force at \(q_1\) plus the spring force at \(q_2\). The same for the damper and the inertia. So the sum of the motions balances the sum of the forces. The pieces do not disturb each other. In the book: 9.1.5, lemma 9.6.

Here we used the assumption the whole of today's part stands on: linearity. We used it when stacking \(q_1\) and \(q_2\). Why it holds: for small motions the spring force and the damper force are proportional to displacement and speed, and for A the displacements are only a few millimetres, for example \(4.0\) mm on a cantilever \(1\) m long. When not: with dry friction, at large pendulum angles, with a weight that lifts off its support. What it does to the result: the answers then do not add and the formula has no meaning. This is not a small error, it is the wrong road.

3.4 Why does \(h(t - s)\) stand in the integral?

One last step. The blow came at time \(s\), and we watch the cantilever at time \(t\). Which part of its swing do we see then? The swing set off by a blow at time \(s\) has been going on for \(t - s\) by time \(t\). So it contributes its swing at that age. In the picture with two blows the second blow at \(0.16\) s is only \(0.05\) s old at the instant \(0.21\) s, the first is \(0.21\) s old. That is all \(t - s\) means: we count the time since each blow.

How do we see this on a single graph? Each column of the picture is one time \(t\), and each has three axes. At the top we draw the force \(Q(s)\), this time a longer wave that lasts \(0.5\) s. On the same axes we also draw \(h(t - s)\): the swing \(h\), mirrored so that its start lands at \(s = t\). Why mirrored? Because the youngest blow, just before \(t\), is only at the start of its swing, while the oldest is at its end. This curve is a weight: how much of the blow at time \(s\) is still in motion at time \(t\). In the middle we multiply the force and the weight. The positive parts and the negative parts of the product add up to an area, and that area is the displacement. At the bottom is the response \(q\), and each dot is the area from the same column. In the book: 9.10.5.

How far back does this memory reach? Let us look again at the lower graph of the envelope. For A it falls to a tenth after \(6.5\) s and to a hundredth after \(13.0\) s. The cantilever remembers past forces, but not forever.

The statement about memory rests on damping. Why it holds: cantilever A has \(\zeta = 0.01\), so \(\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 0.3542\) 1/s. From this number comes the tenth after \(6.5\) s. When not: without damping, \(\zeta = 0\), the envelope stays level and the system forgets nothing. The strip sum still holds then.

3.5 From the ground back to the top

Now we have the ground: force times a short time is a change of momentum, after the blow the system is alone, proportional things add, time is counted from the blow. Let us build back up. We return to the first picture. We cut the force into strips. Each strip is a blow with impulse \(Q(s_{\mathrm{j}})\,\Delta s\), the area of the strip (first step). Each blow sets off a swing \(h\), which at time \(t\) is \(t - s_{\mathrm{j}}\) old (second and fourth steps). We add the swings (third step) and get the sum. As the strips get thinner, the sum becomes the integral.

One more assumption is in this sum: the system is at rest at the start. We used it when we added only the responses of the strips. Why it holds: in our examples the force starts on a cantilever at rest, the sum starts at zero. When not: when the cantilever is already swinging at the start. What it does: we add the free swing from the starting values, the first term of equation (9.100). This term decays with the same envelope and for A falls to a hundredth after \(13.0\) s.

Let us say honestly what the book does. The strip sum is the idea, not a proof, since each strip is a blow only approximately. The book therefore writes the integral as a candidate, checks that it really solves the equation, and concludes from the uniqueness of the solution that it is the only one. In the book: theorem 9.96, equation (9.100).

3.6 The hammer view

Whoever has only a few minutes should remember the picture with two blows. A hammer taps the cantilever, each tap starts its own ringing. Each ringing goes on as if the others were not there, and what we see is their sum. Any force is just a very dense row of very small taps.

3.7 The view by numbers

How coarse may the strips be? In the first picture there are only six. The sum gives a displacement of \(0.16803\) mm at \(t = 0.3\) s, the integral \(0.16793\) mm. Let us write how the difference shrinks with denser strips:

number of strips \(2\) \(4\) \(6\) \(8\) \(16\)
deviation from the integral \(+0.73\) % \(+0.14\) % \(+0.06\) % \(+0.033\) % \(+0.0082\) %

Already six strips, each \(\Delta s = 0.0148\) s long, less than a tenth of \(T_{\mathrm{n}}\), hit the integral to \(0.06\) %. In the book: 9.10.1 and 9.10.7, where the same sum is also built from measured samples of the force.

3.8 The view by frequency

The same system can be described twice. On the left is the impulse response \(h\), which decays with its envelope and has a memory of \(1/(\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}}) = 2.823\) s. On the right is the response to cosines from the second part, with its peak at the natural frequency, about \(2\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) wide. A long memory and a narrow peak are the same property, seen once in time and once in frequency. A force that repeats is a sum of cosines, and the system answers most strongly to the one that falls into the narrow peak. In the book: 9.12.

3.9 Resonance seen in time

Now we can explain the second part from the side of time.

We draw two time axes. At the top we strike twice with the same blow, the second time exactly one natural period \(T_{\mathrm{n}}\) later. Each blow sets off its own swing. The second swing starts just when the first is back at the start of its wave, so they are in step. The sum peaks at \(5.4\) mm, almost twice the first peak, \(2.8\) mm. Why not exactly twice? Because in one period the first swing has decayed by damping to \(0.939\) of its size, and \(1 + 0.939 = 1.939\).

At the bottom we strike the same way, but the second time after only half a period. Then the first swing is coming back down while the second starts upwards. The swings are out of step and the sum stays below \(0.09\) mm. A cosine with the right rhythm sends blows whose swings all arrive in step, so they grow. A cosine with another rhythm sends blows that cancel each other. That is the resonance of the second part, now seen in time.
